extracted.intended_audience: readers of History News Network; general public, historians, journalists and others interested in academic integrity and media controversies
extracted.subtask_description: A chronological compilation and running account of the 2002 Doris Kearns Goodwin plagiarism scandal, documenting reports, responses, editorial decisions, institutional actions, and arguments about standards of attribution and scholarship. The page aggregates media items, quotes, and examples used to evaluate whether Goodwin's work met scholarly and journalistic standards.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dictionary definition of plagiarism
rubrics_metrics.description: Plagiarism defined (Webster): 'to steal and pass off as one's own (the ideas or words of another); use (a created production) without crediting the source ... to commit literary theft: present as new and original an idea or product derived from an existing source.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used by commentators (Jonathan Yardley quoted) to argue that Goodwin's conduct fits traditional definitions of plagiarism; serves as an evaluative baseline for judging alleged copying. Example: critics cite Webster to support labeling Goodwin's actions 'plagiarize.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Harvard policy on suspected plagiarism and consequences
rubrics_metrics.description: Harvard policy (as cited) 'requires instructors to report all suspected cases to the Dean of the College,' with most cases adjudicated by the Administrative Board; if the majority believe sources were misused, they 'will likely vote that you be required to withdraw from the College for at least two semesters.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used as a comparative standard in debates about how professionals should be held accountable; critics argued that professionals should face consequences similar to students, while others noted differences in context and role. Example: Timothy Noah's argument that a Harvard freshman would face severe punishment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appropriate credit to the source (attribution standard)
rubrics_metrics.description: The controlling standard for proper scholarly practice is 'providing appropriate credit to the source.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Goodwin repeatedly invoked the need to credit sources; commentators and critics assessed whether footnotes, endnotes, or text attributions met this standard. Example: Goodwin's statement that 'the most important thing ... is providing appropriate credit to the source.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Quotation marks vs footnotes: visible attribution practices
rubrics_metrics.description: Proper attribution includes not only footnotes but also accurate use of quotation marks for exact language; failing to use quotation marks around verbatim passages can constitute improper attribution even if sources are footnoted.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Debate centered on whether adding footnotes retroactively addressed copying of whole passages without quotation marks. Critics pointed out that adding a footnote does not cure the presence of unattributed verbatim or near-verbatim passages. Example: McTaggert and Noah arguing that footnotes did not change the fact that many passages remained as if they were Goodwin's own words.

rubrics_metrics.name: Substantiality/volume standard
rubrics_metrics.description: The amount or volume of borrowed material is a key factor: large-scale borrowing ('thousands of words' or numerous similar passages/pages) supports claims of infringement or serious appropriation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: McTaggert's claim that Goodwin copied 'thousands of my exact or nearly exact words' and counts of pages/phrases were used as evidence. The LA Times' sampling found nearly three dozen instances of resemblance in No Ordinary Time. Substantiality informs judgments of severity and whether conduct is accidental or systematic.

rubrics_metrics.name: Intent versus negligence in evaluating misconduct
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether copying was deliberate intent to deceive or the result of careless note-taking and error affects moral/political judgment, though some institutional policies (e.g., Harvard's) may not treat intent as dispositive.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Lawrence Tribe and others argued Goodwin lacked intent to deceive; critics (e.g., Timothy Noah) noted institutional rules may punish regardless of intent and that intent does not fully excuse large-scale appropriation. Use caution: intent influences sympathy and sanction severity but does not negate the existence of copied material.

rubrics_metrics.name: Authorial responsibility and researcher cross-checking
rubrics_metrics.description: Authors bear ultimate responsibility for verifying quotations and attributions, even when using researchers or research assistants.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Goodwin blamed note-taking and researcher cross-check failures but also accepted responsibility: 'That was her responsibility to cross-check it, but it was Goodwin's book? ... But that doesn't matter. It's mine. I'm the one.' The standard implies that employing researchers does not absolve an author of ensuring accurate attribution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Publisher remediation and correction practices
rubrics_metrics.description: Publishers are expected to take remedial steps when errors are discovered, such as withdrawing/pulping copies, issuing corrected editions, or destroying existing stock, and to be transparent about corrections.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Goodwin said Simon & Schuster would destroy copies and publish a corrected edition at a cost; later reporting (Alex Beam) found copies without corrections still on sale, raising questions about follow-through. Guidance: publishers should follow through on stated corrections and be clear about which editions are corrected.

rubrics_metrics.name: Institutional and professional consequences
rubrics_metrics.description: Institutions and organizations may respond to proven or alleged plagiarism by withdrawing invitations, putting individuals on leave, rescinding speaking engagements, requesting resignations from boards, or conducting investigations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples include PBS placing Goodwin on indefinite leave from The NewsHour, multiple universities rescinding speaking invitations, withdrawal from the Pulitzer panel, and eventual resignation from the Pulitzer board. Such actions reflect reputational, professional, and institutional sanctions short of legal remedies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clear labeling of satire and editorial responsibility
rubrics_metrics.description: Editors and publications must clearly label satirical pieces to avoid misleading readers and conflating satire with factual reporting.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The NYT published a satirical piece that many readers mistook for fact; the Times later issued a correction acknowledging insufficient labeling. This is an editorial-standard criterion for responsible journalism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transparency of evidence and editorial 'work product' decisions
rubrics_metrics.description: When a news organization finds parallels or evidence of copying, editorial decisions about releasing underlying evidence (e.g., lists of parallels) affect public ability to judge the gravity of allegations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The LA Times declined to publish the 30-odd parallels its researcher found, calling them 'work product'; critics (Philip Nobile) argued the paper had an obligation to reveal its evidence so readers could judge severity. This raises a standard about balancing reporting practice and transparency.

rubrics_metrics.name: Paraphrasing, common phrasing, and necessary shared wording
rubrics_metrics.description: Some overlap in phrasing may be acceptable—common expressions or necessary adherence to chronology/structure may constrain rewording—but such reuse still requires clear attribution.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Goodwin's defense invoked common expressions and the need to preserve chronology ('sequential action was being described'), arguing some similarity is inevitable; critics countered that similarity plus lack of quotation marks or attribution could still be inappropriate. Assessors should weigh whether the similarity is unavoidable/common or represents borrowing that should have been quoted or paraphrased with credit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Copyright infringement as a separate standard from plagiarism
rubrics_metrics.description: Copyright claims rest on whether exact or nearly exact words were appropriated in quantities sufficient to infringe the author's copyright, distinct from or overlapping with academic plagiarism.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: McTaggert argued a copyright infringement claim based on 'thousands of exact or nearly exact words' and page-by-page comparisons; copyright analysis may involve counting instances and assessing substantial similarity beyond scholarly credit norms.
